source_text: MULTA et magna sunt, fratres charissimi beneficia divina quibus in salutem nostram Dei Patris et Christi larga et copiosa clementia et operata sit et semper operetur, quod conservandis ac vivificandis nobis Pater Filium misit, ut reparare nos posset, quodque Filius missus esse et hominis filius fieri voluit ut nos Dei filios faceret. Humiliavit se, ut populum qui prius jacebat erigeret: vulneratus est, ut vulnera nostra curaret: servivit, ut ad libertatem servientes extraheret: mori sustinuit, ut immortalitatem mortalibus exhiberet. Multa haec sunt et magna divinae misericordiae munera. Sed adhuc, qualis providentia illa et quanta clementia est quod nobis salutari ratione prospicitur, ut homini qui redemptus est reservando plenius consulatur! Nam, cum Dominus adveniens sanasset illa quae Adam portaverat vulnera, et venena serpentis antiqua curasset, legem dedit sano, et praecepit ne ultra jam peccaret, ne quid peccanti gravius eveniret. Coarctati eramus et in angustum innocentiae praescriptione conclusi. Nec haberet quid fragilitatis humanae infirmitas atque imbecillitas faceret, nisi iterum pietas divina subveniens, justitiae et misericordiae operibus ostensis, viam quamdam tuendae salutis aperiret, ut sordes postmodum, quascumque contrahimus, eleemosynis abluamus. Loquitur in Scripturis divinis Spiritus sanctus et dicit: Eleemosynis et fide delicta purgantur. Non utique illa delicta quae fuerant ante contracta, nam illa Christi sanguine et sanctificatione purgantur. Item denuo dicit: Sicut aqua extinguit ignem, sic eleemosyna extinguit peccatum. Hic quoque ostenditur et probatur quia, sicut lavacro aquae salutaris gehennae ignis extinguitur, ita et eleemosynis atque operationibus justis delictorum flamma sopitur. Et quia semel in Baptismo remissa peccatorum datur, assidua et jugis operatio Baptismi instar imitata, Dei rursus indulgentiam largitur. Hoc et in Evangelio Dominus docet. Nam cum denotarentur discipuli ejus quod ederent, nec prius manus abluissent, respondit et dixit: Qui fecit quod intus est, fecit et quod foris est. Verum date eleemosynam, et ecce vobis munda omnia: docens scilicet et ostendens non manus lavandas esse, sed pectus, et sordes intrinsecus potius quam extrinsecus detrahendas; verum qui purgaverit quod est intus, eum quoque id quod foris est repurgasse, et emundata mente, cute quoque et corpore mundum esse coepisse. Porro autem, monens et ostendens unde mundi et purgati esse possimus, addidit eleemosynas esse faciendas. Misericors docet et monet misericordiam fieri; et quia servare quaerit quos magno pretio redemit, post Baptismi gratiam sordidatos docet denuo posse purgari. Agnoscamus itaque, fratres charissimi, divinae indulgentiae munus salubre, et emundandis purgandisque peccatis nostris, qui sine aliquo conscientiae vulnere esse non possumus, medelis spiritalibus vulnera nostra curemus. Nec quisquam sic sibi de puro atque immaculato pectore blandiatur, ut, innocentia sua fretus, medicinam non putet adhibendam esse vulneribus, cum scriptum sit: Quis gloriabitur castum se habere cor, aut quis gloriabitur mundum se esse a peccatis? et iterum in Epistola sua Joannes ponat et dicat: Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos decipimus, et veritas in nobis non est. Si autem nemo esse sine peccato potest, et quisquis inculpatum se esse dixerit, aut superbus aut stultus est, quam necessaria, quam benigna est divina clementia, quae, cum sciat non deesse sanatis quaedam postmodum vulnera, dedit curandis denuo sanandisque vulneribus remedia salutaria! Numquam denique, fratres dilectissimi, admonitio divina cessavit et tacuit quominus in Scripturis sanctis tam veteribus quam novis semper et ubique ad misericordiae opera Dei populus provocaretur; et canente atque exhortante Spiritu sancto, quisquis ad spem regni coelestis instruitur, facere eleemosynas jubetur. Mandat et praecipit Esaiae Deus: Exclama, inquit, in fortitudine, et noli parcere. Sicut tuba exalta vocem tuam, et annuntia plebi meae peccata ipsorum et domui Jacob facinora eorum. Et cum peccata eis sua exprobrari praecepisset, cumque eorum facinora pleno indignationis impetu protulisset, dixissetque eos nec, si orationibus et precibus et jejuniis uterentur, satisfacere pro delictis posse, nec, si in cilicio et cinere volverentur, iram Dei posse lenire, in novissima tamen parte, demonstrans solis eleemosynis Deum posse placari, addidit dicens: Frange esurienti panem tuum, et egenos sine tecto induc in domum tuam. Si videris nudum, vesti eum, et domesticos seminis tui non despicias. Tunc erumpet temporaneum lumen tuum, et vestimenta tua cito orientur, et praeibit ante te justitia, et claritas Dei circumdabit te. Tunc exclamabis, et Deus exaudiet te. Dum adhuc loqueris dicet: Ecce adsum.
pass_a_gloss: Many and great are the divine benefits by which God the Father and Christ have worked and are working for our salvation, because the Father sent the Son to preserve and give life to us, and the Son willed to be sent and to become the son of man so that he might make us sons of God. He humbled himself so that he might raise up the people who were previously lying down, he was wounded so that he might heal our wounds, he served so that he might lead servants to freedom, he endured death so that he might show immortality to mortals. These are many and great gifts of divine mercy. But moreover, what kind of providence and how great is the mercy by which we are looked after for our salvation, so that the person who has been redeemed may be more fully advised? For when the Lord came and healed the wounds that Adam had borne, and cured the ancient poisons of the serpent, he gave a law to the healthy and commanded that they not sin again, lest something worse happen to the sinner. We were constrained and enclosed in a narrow prescription of innocence. And human fragility and weakness would have nothing to do, unless divine piety, assisting again, showed works of justice and mercy and opened a certain way of preserving salvation, so that we might wash away the filth that we contract afterwards with alms. The Holy Spirit speaks in the divine Scriptures and says: Sins are purified by alms and faith. Not those sins which were contracted before, for those are purified by the blood and sanctification of Christ. Again, he says: Just as water extinguishes fire, so alms extinguish sin. Here also it is shown and proven that just as the fire of Gehenna is extinguished by the bath of saving water, so also the flame of sins is calmed by alms and just works. And because once in Baptism the remission of sins is given, a constant and daily operation, imitating Baptism, again obtains God's indulgence. The Lord also teaches this in the Gospel. For when his disciples were denoted as eating without washing their hands, he responded and said: He who made what is inside also made what is outside. But give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you, teaching and showing that it is not the hands that need to be washed, but the breast, and that the filth inside rather than outside needs to be removed. And he who has purified what is inside has also repurified what is outside, and with a cleansed mind, he has also begun to be clean in body and skin. Furthermore, warning and showing from where we can be clean and purified, he added that alms need to be done. The merciful one teaches and warns to do mercy, and because he seeks to preserve those whom he redeemed at a great price, after the grace of Baptism, he teaches that those who have been stained can again be purified. Let us therefore recognize, most dear brothers, the salutary gift of divine indulgence, and let us cure our wounds with spiritual remedies, we who cannot be without any wound of conscience. And let no one flatter himself about having a pure and immaculate breast, so that, trusting in his own innocence, he does not think that medicine needs to be applied to wounds, since it is written: Who will boast that he has a chaste heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sins? And again, John puts it in his Epistle and says: If we say that we do not have sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if no one can be without sin, and whoever says that he is blameless is either proud or foolish, how necessary, how kind is divine mercy, which, knowing that the healthy do not lack some wounds afterwards, gave remedies for healing and saving wounds again! Finally, most beloved brothers, divine admonition has never ceased and been silent, so that in the holy Scriptures, both old and new, the people of God may always and everywhere be provoked to works of mercy, and with the Holy Spirit singing and exhorting, whoever is instructed to the hope of the heavenly kingdom is commanded to do alms. God commands and orders in Isaiah: Cry out, he says, with strength, and do not spare. Just as a trumpet raises its voice, announce to my people their sins and to the house of Jacob their crimes. And when he had commanded that their sins be reproached to them, and their crimes be brought forth with a full impulse of indignation, and had said that they could not satisfy for their sins even with prayers and supplications and fasts, nor could they placate the wrath of God even if they rolled in sackcloth and ashes, nonetheless, in the last part, showing that God can be placated only by alms, he added, saying: Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and homeless into your house. If you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise the members of your family. Then your light will break forth, and your garments will quickly arise, and justice will go before you, and the glory of God will surround you. Then you will cry out, and God will hear you. While you are still speaking, he will say: Behold, I am present.

bible_refs.note: Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the needy and homeless into your house
But give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you

pass_b_english: God the Father and Christ have worked and continue to work countless, great divine benefits for our salvation. The Father sent the Son to preserve us and give us life, and the Son willingly was sent and became the son of man so that he might make us sons of God. He humbled himself to raise up the people who had been lying low; he was wounded to heal our wounds; he served to lead servants out into freedom; he endured death to offer immortality to mortals. These are many and great gifts of divine mercy.

Yet consider what kind of providence and how great a mercy looks after us for our salvation, so that the redeemed person may be more fully provided for. When the Lord came, he healed the wounds that Adam had borne and cured the ancient poisons of the serpent. He gave a law to the healthy and commanded them not to sin again, lest something worse befall the sinner. We were constrained and shut up in a narrow prescription of innocence. Human fragility and weakness would have had no recourse unless divine pity came to our aid again, displayed works of justice and mercy, and opened a way to preserve our salvation — so that we might wash away whatever filth we contract afterward by means of alms.

The Holy Spirit speaks in the divine Scriptures and says: “Sins are purified by alms and faith” (Prov 16:6). Not those sins contracted earlier, for those are purified by the blood and sanctification of Christ. Again he says: “Just as water extinguishes fire, so alms extinguishes sin” (Sir 3:30). Here it is also shown and proven that just as the fire of Gehenna is extinguished by the bath of saving water, so the flame of sins is calmed by alms and just works. Because the remission of sins is given once in Baptism, a constant and daily practice that imitates Baptism obtains God's indulgence again.

The Lord teaches this in the Gospel as well (Luke 11:41). When his disciples were criticized for eating without first washing their hands, he answered: “The one who made the inside also made the outside. But give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you.” He was teaching and showing that it is not the hands that need washing, but the heart, and that the filth inside rather than outside must be removed. Whoever has purified what is inside has also repurified what is outside, and with a cleansed mind has begun to be clean in body and skin as well.

Furthermore, warning us and showing from what source we can become clean and purified, he added that alms must be done. The Merciful One teaches and urges mercy to be done; because he seeks to preserve those whom he redeemed at great cost, he teaches that after the grace of Baptism, those who have been stained can be purified again.

Let us therefore recognize, dearest brothers, the salutary gift of divine indulgence. We who cannot be without some wound of conscience, let us cure our wounds with spiritual remedies. No one should flatter himself about having a pure and immaculate heart so that, trusting his own innocence, he thinks medicine need not be applied to wounds. Scripture says: “Who will boast that he has a chaste heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sins?” (Prov 20:9). And again John writes in his Epistle: “If we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). If no one can be without sin, and whoever claims to be blameless is either proud or foolish, how necessary, how kind is divine mercy! Knowing that the healthy do not lack some wounds afterward, it gave remedies for healing and saving wounds again.

Finally, dearest brothers, divine admonition has never ceased or been silent. In the holy Scriptures, both old and new, the people of God are always and everywhere provoked to works of mercy. With the Holy Spirit singing and exhorting, whoever is instructed toward the hope of the heavenly kingdom is commanded to give alms.

God commands and orders in Isaiah: “Cry out with strength, and do not spare. Like a trumpet raise your voice; announce to my people their sins and to the house of Jacob their crimes” (Isa 58:1). After commanding that their sins be reproached to them and their crimes be laid bare with full indignation, and after saying that they could not satisfy for their sins even with prayers, supplications, and fasts, nor placate God’s wrath even by rolling in sackcloth and ashes, nonetheless in the final passage he shows that God can be placated only by alms. He adds: “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house. If you see the naked, clothe him, and do not despise your own kin” (Isa 58:6-7). “Then your light shall break forth like the dawn, and your healing shall spring up quickly; your righteousness shall go before you, the glory of the Lord shall be your rear guard. Then you shall call, and the Lord will answer; you shall cry, and he will say, Here I am” (Isa 58:8-9).

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text. Scripture citations in Pass B (Prov 16:6, Sir 3:30, Luke 11:41, Prov 20:9, 1 John 1:8, Isa 58:1, Isa 58:6-7, Isa 58:8-9) correctly identify the biblical sources alluded to in the Latin, even where the Latin does not explicitly name the book (e.g., the 'Scripturis divinis' and 'Evangelio' references). Pass A and B are consistent with the Latin source.
